explanation_text: The Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple stand in a line, each with its own height and position. In the same way, the place of a digit—ones, tens, hundreds—decides the value it holds.
image_prompt: Illustrate the Three Pagodas of Dali standing in a row, each labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds to show how position decides value.

explanation_text: When more fishing boats gather on Erhai Lake, the count on the water grows. When some boats sail away, it shrinks—just like addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: Show fishing boats gathering on Erhai Lake (increasing the count) and a boat sailing away (decreasing it), with plus and minus signs.

explanation_text: Rows of tie-dyed cloth hung out to dry form equal groups, showing multiplication. Dividing the cloth evenly among the dyers shows division.
image_prompt: Display equal rows of tie-dyed cloth hanging on a line, showing equal grouping (multiplication) and even sharing (division).

explanation_text: Dancers at the Torch Festival pair up to perform; when every dancer has a partner, the number is even. If one dancer stands alone, the number is odd.
image_prompt: Show Torch Festival dancers standing in pairs, with one single dancer at the end to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: The painted patterns that decorate whitewashed Bai house walls repeat in regular sequences. Counting every fifth motif is like skip counting by 5.
image_prompt: Show a repeating painted pattern on a white Bai house wall, highlighting every 5th motif to illustrate skip counting.

explanation_text: The bowls of Bai three-course tea hold different amounts. Comparing their levels shows which is greater or smaller, just like comparing numbers.
image_prompt: Show three tea bowls with different amounts of three-course tea, using > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: At the March Street fair, cooks estimate how much rice to prepare for the expected crowd. Estimating a close, convenient amount is like rounding.
image_prompt: Show a cook estimating rice portions at the March Street fair, labeled with rounded amounts.

explanation_text: Three-course tea is served in small bowls shared among the guests. Each guest receives a portion, or fraction, of the whole serving.
image_prompt: Show a pot of three-course tea being divided into equal small bowls, each labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: Cutting a round ba ba flatbread into 2 equal pieces, then each piece into 2 again, gives 4 equal pieces of the same total. Halves and quarters name the same amount—like equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a round ba ba flatbread divided first into halves, then quarters, demonstrating equal portions.

explanation_text: Many small groups of butterflies gather into one swarm at Butterfly Spring. Combining small groups into one whole is like simplifying a fraction to its lowest terms.
image_prompt: Depict small groups of butterflies merging into one large swarm, labeled with reduced fractions.

explanation_text: If a farmer has 3 full baskets of rice and half a basket more, that is 3½ baskets. A whole part together with a fraction is a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full rice baskets and one half-full basket labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When rice fills one basket and continues into a second, the amount is greater than one whole basket. Measured in same-sized parts, it is an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show rice spilling from a full basket into another basket, symbolizing fractions greater than 1.

explanation_text: Pouring the leftover tea from several small bowls into one bowl shows how fractional amounts add together to make a whole.
image_prompt: Show smaller bowls of three-course tea being poured together to make one total bowl.

bai_culture: Leaving part of a tea cup
explanation_text: When a guest drinks part of a cup of three-course tea, the amount remaining is the total minus the fraction that was drunk.
image_prompt: Show a cup of three-course tea with part of it drunk, the remainder labeled as the fraction left.

bai_culture: Half of a rice cake piece
explanation_text: If a guest takes half of a half piece of rice cake, they get a quarter. Finding a fraction of a fraction is multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: Show a plate of rice cake divided into halves, and one half divided again to show smaller portions.

explanation_text: Cutting a portion of rice cake into smaller equal pieces shows how many smaller fractions fit into one portion—that is dividing fractions.
image_prompt: Show rice cake being cut into smaller even pieces to illustrate fractional division.

explanation_text: Measuring the tea brewed for three-course tea in liters introduces decimals, such as 1.5 liters meaning one and a half liters.
image_prompt: Show a measuring pot marked with 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters of tea.

explanation_text: Whether a bowl holds half a liter or 0.5 liters, both describe the same amount. Naming one amount two ways is converting between fractions and decimals.
image_prompt: Show two labeled bowls, one marked ½ and another 0.5, filled with the same amount of tea.

explanation_text: When a student scores 85 out of 100 on a test at a Dali school, that is 85%. Percents express parts per hundred.
image_prompt: Show a test paper with 85/100 written and an 85% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A 20% discount on a tie-dyed cloth at the March Street fair shows how percents are used to find a part of a price.
image_prompt: Show a stall sign at the March Street fair with tie-dyed cloth marked '20% off' and reduced price tags.

explanation_text: In a teahouse, some jars hold tea of unknown amounts. An unlabeled jar stands for an unknown quantity, just like a variable in math.
image_prompt: Show labeled tea jars (1L, 2L) and an unlabeled jar marked as x.

explanation_text: If a shelf holds 2 known jars of tea and x more unlabeled ones, the total is written as 2 + x. Combining known and unknown amounts is an expression.
image_prompt: Show two tea jars plus an unlabeled one, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: A Bai farmer carries baskets at both ends of a shoulder pole; when the two sides balance, the weights are equal. Both sides of an equation hold the same value, just like the balanced baskets.
image_prompt: Show a carrying pole with equal baskets on both ends, labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If one basket on a carrying pole is heavier, the farmer adds or removes a little weight to restore balance. One small adjustment solves the load, like a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a carrying pole with baskets, one side adjusted by adding or removing weight to show a one-step equation.

explanation_text: Brewing three-course tea needs two moves: first roast the tea leaves, then add boiling water. Solving a two-step equation also works through two operations in order.
image_prompt: Show the two-step sequence of brewing three-course tea—roast the leaves, then add water—symbolizing step-by-step solving.

explanation_text: When one family's rice harvest is larger than another's, the amounts are unequal. Greater than and less than compare harvests just as they compare numbers.
image_prompt: Show two piles of harvested rice of different sizes with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: When cooking a Bai dish, you must prepare the ingredients before steaming and serve the courses in order. The order of steps matters, exactly as it does with the order of operations.
image_prompt: Show a cooking sequence for a Bai dish where steps must happen in order, labeled like parentheses, exponents, and so on.

explanation_text: When a weaver's shuttle wears out, an identical new one takes its place and weaving continues. Replacing a variable with its value works the same way.
image_prompt: Show a missing shuttle replaced with an identical one in a loom, representing substitution.

explanation_text: Each star in the night sky above Erhai Lake marks a single position. A point in geometry is just such a location on a plane.
image_prompt: Show a starry sky over Erhai Lake with individual stars labeled as points on a coordinate grid.

explanation_text: The stretched threads used to tie tie-dye cloth run straight in both directions. Straight lines in geometry extend the same way.
image_prompt: Show straight threads stretched for tie-dye, representing geometric lines.

explanation_text: As a door of a Bai house swings open, it forms an angle with the door frame. The size of the opening measures that angle.
image_prompt: Show a Bai house door partially open with the angle clearly marked.

explanation_text: The vertical pillars and horizontal beams of a Bai house meet at right angles. Lines that cross at 90 degrees are perpendicular.
image_prompt: Show the pillars and beams of a Bai house meeting at 90° angles.

explanation_text: The ridges between rice paddies run side by side and never meet, all the way to the far edge of the field. Parallel lines behave the same way.
image_prompt: Show two parallel ridges between rice paddies running side by side through the field.

explanation_text: The stone slabs paving the streets of Dali old town form closed shapes with many sides. Closed many-sided figures are polygons.
image_prompt: Show stone slabs in the streets of Dali old town forming closed geometric shapes.

explanation_text: Seen against the sky, each pagoda of the Three Pagodas narrows toward the top, tracing a triangular silhouette. A triangle is a three-sided shape.
image_prompt: Show the triangular silhouettes of the Three Pagodas of Dali against the sky.

explanation_text: The painted patterns on whitewashed Bai house walls include squares and rectangles. Four-sided shapes are quadrilaterals.
image_prompt: Show a Bai house wall with repeating square and rectangular painted motifs.

explanation_text: Walking all the way around the old town wall of Dali measures its whole outline. The distance around a shape is its perimeter.
image_prompt: Show people walking around the old town wall of Dali with a dashed perimeter line.

explanation_text: Farmers measure how much of the lakeside plain their rice paddies cover. The space inside a flat shape is its area.
image_prompt: Show rice paddies spread beside Erhai Lake, shaded to show their area.

explanation_text: A Bai home keeps water in large jars, each holding a fixed amount. The space inside a container is its volume.
image_prompt: Show large water jars filled to different levels to illustrate volume.

explanation_text: Seen from above, Butterfly Spring forms a nearly perfect circle. Its radius, diameter, and circumference can all be measured, as for any circle.
image_prompt: Show Butterfly Spring from above labeled with radius and diameter lines.

explanation_text: The round millstone used to grind rice has a circumference and a diameter. Whatever the stone's size, circumference divided by diameter is always π.
image_prompt: Show a round millstone labeled with its circumference and diameter measurements.

explanation_text: The streets of Dali old town cross in rows and columns like a grid, and every corner has a fixed location. A coordinate plane places points with x- and y-values the same way.
image_prompt: Show a map of Dali old town streets labeled with x and y coordinates.

explanation_text: Marking the position of each house on a map of a Dali village places every home at a precise spot. That is plotting points on a coordinate plane.
image_prompt: Show a map of a Dali village with each house marked as a labeled point.

explanation_text: On a calm day, the Three Pagodas are reflected perfectly in the water of Erhai Lake below. The reflection matches the real scene across a line—that is symmetry.
image_prompt: Show the Three Pagodas and their reflection in the water, split by a mirror line.

explanation_text: Dancers at the Torch Festival spin, slide, and change formation, shifting every position without breaking the pattern. Moving and turning shapes are geometric transformations.
image_prompt: Show Torch Festival dancers turning and shifting positions to illustrate transformations.

explanation_text: Three-course tea balances bitter, sweet, and aftertaste; the amounts of tea leaves and water follow a fixed ratio. Ratios compare two quantities.
image_prompt: Show a teapot labeled with tea-to-water ratios, like 2:1.

explanation_text: When a weaver copies a small tie-dye pattern onto a larger cloth, every part grows by the same factor. Keeping all parts in the same relationship is proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small and a large tie-dye cloth with the same pattern proportions.

explanation_text: At the March Street fair, tea is priced per jin, so the cost of one jin is a unit rate. Unit rates compare an amount to a single unit.
image_prompt: Show a March Street tea stall with prices marked per jin (yuan per jin).

explanation_text: A small map can show the whole old town of Dali because every distance is shrunk by the same scale. Drawing a place smaller while keeping ratios is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show Dali old town and a smaller scaled map beside it with a scale legend.

explanation_text: If a family's rice harvest rises from 100 to 120 jin, that is a 20% increase. Percent change measures how much an amount grows or shrinks.
image_prompt: Show harvested rice piles growing in size with a +20% label.

explanation_text: At the March Street fair, traders record how many items of each kind they sell each day. Gathering and recording numbers is data collection.
image_prompt: Show a trader marking tallies of sales on a clipboard at the March Street fair.

explanation_text: A graph showing how much rice each season brings in helps farmers compare the year's harvests at a glance. Tables and graphs turn data into pictures.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph comparing rice harvests across the four seasons.

explanation_text: Adding a fisher's catches over several days and dividing by the number of days gives the average catch. The average is the mean.
image_prompt: Show a table of daily fish catches on Erhai with the average value highlighted.

explanation_text: When household incomes in a Dali village are lined up from smallest to largest, the value in the middle is the median.
image_prompt: Show household incomes lined up with the middle one highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: Most tie-dyed cloth is dyed indigo blue, so indigo is the most frequent color. The value that appears most often is the mode.
image_prompt: Show bolts of tie-dyed cloth in various colors with indigo blue being the most common.

explanation_text: The gap between the largest and smallest rice harvest in a village shows how spread out the data is. The highest value minus the lowest is the range.
image_prompt: Show a bar chart with the shortest and tallest harvest bars marked for range.

explanation_text: Each bar can show how much rice one family harvested, making the harvests easy to compare. Bar graphs compare amounts by length.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph labeled by family names with their rice harvest totals.

explanation_text: A line graph can trace how rainfall changes month by month beside Erhai Lake. Line graphs show how a quantity changes over time.
image_prompt: Show a line graph labeled with months and rainfall amounts.

explanation_text: A pie chart can show what share of the Dali plains is planted in rice, vegetables, and other crops. Each slice shows a part of the whole.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart divided into crop categories with percentages.

bai_culture: Winners of the Erhai boat race
explanation_text: Before an Erhai boat race, guessing which boat is most likely to win involves probability. Probability measures how likely an event is.
image_prompt: Show dragon boats at a race start line on Erhai with probability labels above each.

explanation_text: The painted borders around Bai house walls repeat the same motifs over and over. Repeated designs are patterns, in art and in numbers alike.
image_prompt: Show repeating painted border motifs on the walls of a Bai house.

explanation_text: At a fixed time, each boat speed on Erhai gives one exact distance. A function pairs every input with a single output, just as each speed gives one distance.
image_prompt: Show a graph linking boat speed (input) to distance traveled (output) on Erhai Lake.
